drills.q: A teammate says 'we keep our prompts in git, that's versioning.' What does git alone NOT give you, and what does the pipeline add?
drills.a: Git gives diff, review, blame — storage. It does not give delivery: no staged rollout (1% -> 10% -> 100% with sticky hash split), no auto-revert without a deploy, no instant promote for non-code owners, and prompt iteration cadence ends up coupled to the deploy train. The pipeline adds: eval gate on every diff (new >= old - epsilon), online guardrails per version, and rollback as a label repoint (<1 min, no build).

drills.q: Walk through the promote gate: what must be true before a prompt version goes from staged to a wider rollout?
drills.a: Eval gate passed: new_score >= old_score - epsilon, where epsilon is the eval's own measured jitter (run same version twice, typically 1-3 pts). Then guardrails green at the current stage: task completion, schema-validity >= 99%, cost/step <= 1.15x baseline (excluding post-flip cache warm-up), p95 <= 1.25x. Pre-registered promotion criteria (n per arm, soak time) met — never 'looks fine, advance it'.

drills.q: Why do PATCH bumps (typos) still need the eval gate?
drills.a: Intent is not a guarantee. A formatting change can alter tokenization or attention enough to shift behavior; reordering few-shots is a MINOR bump with real consequences because position in context changes attention; PATCH-level 'cleanups' have regressed double digits. The gate is cheap relative to one silent regression.

drills.q: Your cost guardrail trips 30 minutes into a 100% rollout and auto-reverts a change you believe is good. What happened and how do you fix the guardrail?
drills.a: Post-flip cache warm-up: the new prompt prefix invalidates the old cache, every request pays the 1.25x write on input while the prefix warms, so cost/request spikes briefly. Fix: exclude the first window after any flip from the cost guardrail, or baseline cost in token-equivalents (cache_creation + 0.1x cache_read + uncached) rather than dollars.

drills.q: Canary: 500 requests, 79% completion. Control: 4,500 requests, 83%. Compute the z-score, state your decision, and name the n you'd need to confirm a 4-point drop.
drills.a: SE_canary = sqrt(0.79*0.21/500) ~= 1.8%; SE_control = sqrt(0.83*0.17/4500) ~= 0.56%; SE_diff ~= 1.9%; z = 4/1.9 ~= 2.1 — borderline: revert if policy is 2-sigma hard, else hold one more window. To confirm a 4-point drop at 95%/80% power you need roughly 1,600-1,700 per arm. Note the absolute floor (0.70) has not tripped; this is a relative-tier decision, and it requires n >= 100 per arm minimum.

drills.q: Cache hit rate fell from 90% to near zero overnight. No deploy, no model change. Diagnose.
drills.a: Most likely: someone interpolated a per-request value (current date, user name, tenant id) inside the cached system prefix. The prefix is then unique per request, never matches, and that segment is charged at ~10x the cached rate forever. Both vendors' docs call this the canonical mistake. Fix: static content in the cached prefix, variables after the breakpoint; make cache-hit rate itself a guardrail metric so this pages instead of silently costing.

drills.q: Design the hotfix lane for a PM who needs to ship a wording fix at 18:00 Friday with no deploy.
drills.a: Exists by design or it exists by shadow (someone edits prod directly, once, and you learn from the outage). The lane: 1) still gated — 2-minute fast-eval on a reduced golden slice runs before promote, no exceptions; 2) capped — promotes to 5% traffic, not 100%; 3) timed — 30m-2h auto-expiry back to the previous version unless a human confirms; 4) loud — pages the prompt owner. Saturday cleanup: the hotfix goes through the full gate before 100%.

drills.q: Why is 12 hand-written golden-set items 'gate theater,' and what does a real eval set look like?
drills.a: 12 items catches only catastrophic breakage (schema violations, hard refusals, empty outputs); a 5-point regression on ambiguous cases passes cleanly. Real set: 50-100+ items mined from actual traffic (the Pareto of what users do), adversarial cases (PII, injection, off-topic), verifiers (exact match where possible, judge where not, spot-checked vs human labels), a held-out slice authors never see, and continuous refresh from production. Measure the eval's own jitter by double-running; that spread sets epsilon.

drills.q: One logical prompt runs on Claude, GPT, and an internal model. How do you version it, and what's the failure mode you're preventing?
drills.a: Version the behavioral spec once (inputs, outputs, guardrails, contract) and attach per-model renderings as variants — router@v12[claude], router@v12[gpt] — each rendered from the same spec, each evaled against the same golden set. The failure mode: independent per-model prompt repos that drift independently with no shared definition of 'regression.' 'One universal prompt' is the lowest common denominator, mediocre on every model, and still unstable as vendors change behavior. Honest cost: multi-model triples the eval surface.

drills.q: You're rolling out a prompt registry to 5 teams with 20 prompts. Nobody wants it. What's your adoption sequence, and what's the failure mode of it?
drills.a: 1) Make the loader the easiest path — few-line SDK call with client-side cache so the latency objection dies. 2) Seed it by importing existing prompts WITH history (starts full, not empty). 3) Require it first only for shared prompts, where drift is the demonstrable live failure (two services answering differently is your slide). 4) Show debugging value — trace -> prompt version -> per-version metrics. 5) Only then enforce the gate on direct prod edits. Exempt the two-person team with a stable prompt explicitly. Failure mode: step 1 without step 4 — a pile of unversioned copies in a nicer UI; if nobody queries 'which version was live when this happened' in month two, the rollout is decorative.
